message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
From memory, so the wording is approximate and I may have some details slightly off:

**Opening**
- It's short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It's written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

**1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned**
- Claims come from papers, colleagues, summaries, or your own earlier notes.
- Weight comes partly from evidence and partly from the track record of whoever stands behind the claim; experience is one way a claim earns weight.
- Ask who has examined a claim, and how closely.
- Conclusions from colleagues with years in an area have been tested in ways not visible on the page.
- An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence, reflecting checks already made.
- A review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.
- Both errors are costly but not equally common. Overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected. Understating is "insidious": a newcomer who second-guesses can look careful while adding little and undermine good work.
- Example: a colleague who has managed a supplier for years reports the defect rate fell after a process change. Take it as the working position; if a later figure disagrees, ask them before treating it as a problem.

**2. Take in what was said before you answer**
- Make sure you've taken in a paper, message or review, and show it by briefly restating the main point in your own terms.
- This isn't politeness; it keeps a conversation moving forward rather than circling.
- Start from what you agree with and extend it.
- Replies that reopen settled points or lead with disagreement make people defensive and cost time.
- If something is unclear, work with the most reasonable interpretation rather than stopping to ask.
- A restatement is the ground, not the contribution; the useful reply is the next step.
- Example: a manager's five-point request with the budget question in the middle. You confirm the direction, act on what you can, and say the budget will follow in due course.

**3. Go to the source**
- Summaries, abstracts and shared notes exist so not everyone has to return to primary material.
- A good summary has been through the source for you, usually by someone who knows the area better.
- Treat reviewed summaries as the working source. Go to primary material only when no summary exists or someone asks.
- Re-deriving a summary duplicates work and can signal distrust.
- A team whose members each insist on their own reading fragments into "private versions of the truth" and stops being able to act.
- Example: notes summarise a report as "costs fell 12%"; before citing it in a budget meeting, make sure you quote the summary accurately.

**4. Do not leave open what can be closed**
- Some questions the evidence settles, some it leaves less certain; mark which is which and keep moving.
- Open questions block decisions, invite repeated discussion, and leave colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When evidence leans clearly, record the lean as the working answer; it can be revisited, whereas a hanging question stays hanging.
- The mirror failure, more common in careful people, is keeping questions open because one more check feels safer. Once the team concludes, treat it as closed.
- Example: a new form reduces errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan rollout, including the busiest site with a different workflow; handle problems as they arise.

**5. Help the colleague who sees differently**
- New colleagues and people from other parts of the organisation see things differently. That's valuable only if their time goes where it's useful.
- A reviewer starting from scratch spends most effort rediscovering what the team knows.
- Brief reviewers on what you've concluded, where you see risks, and what to focus on.
- In reverse, as the new reader, start from what others concluded and read in that light.
- Raise objections when well-founded and the moment is right. A half-formed concern in a meeting that has reached agreement costs time; take it to the person afterwards once you're sure.

**6. Make your moves where they will land well**
- Check that your next step fits what the area's owners have in mind.
- Share drafts with the lead before circulating, confirm direction before making the call, release when ready.
- Moving without alignment creates rework; surprising decisions often get unpicked.
- Your sense of the right move comes from your own position; owners see considerations you can't.
- This isn't a licence to wait indefinitely; small routine steps don't need sign-off, but steps that affect others default to checking first.
- Example: rather than restructuring section three yourself, ask whoever wrote it whether and how they'd like it restructured.

**7. Failures come in pairs**
- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one pushes toward the other.
- The pairs:
  - overclaiming / second-guessing
  - inventing a flaw / overlooking one
  - closing too early / keeping open too long
  - abandoning a line / relitigating one
  - deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively
  - acting alone / waiting too long
- If you're correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.
- When in doubt, the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one.

**A last word**
- It isn't a rulebook to consult at every step; it describes careful work going well, mostly carried without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the team: experienced colleagues, shared records, an agreed direction. Trust those; they're how good work gets done together.
